tagline: An automobile crossing of the Berkshires, marked by a summit cairn.
intro: Jacob’s Ladder Trail winds across the Berkshires between the Lee/Lenox town line and Mount Tekoa in Russell, with views of the Westfield River. The route became a Massachusetts Scenic Byway in 1992. Western Massachusetts Scenic Byways highlights its rural landscapes between Laurel Lake and Tekoa Mountain, along with the history of early automobile tourism. On the eastern side, the road follows Walker Brook and the West Branch of the Westfield River through Chester.

Lee resident Cortland Bishop and other Berkshire residents pressed for a good road over the mountains. Jacob’s Ladder Trail opened in September 1910, with a celebration at the summit. Dignitaries and visiting motorists brought rocks from home and piled them there, starting the cairn that marks the crossing. The modern US 20 corridor parallels the Massachusetts Turnpike, which has largely taken over through travel. US 20 continues to serve towns and local business areas that the turnpike bypasses.

From Lee, US 20 heads east into Becket and then Chester. Morey Hill in Becket reaches a 1,775-foot summit. At Chester, the route follows Walker Brook’s valley to the West Branch of the Westfield River. It continues along the river through Huntington toward Russell and the rocky heights of Mount Tekoa.

moments.title: Morey Hill summit
moments.text: The stone cairn at Morey Hill began with rocks carried from other places. Dignitaries and motorists brought them from home to celebrate the road’s September 1910 opening. As many as 4,000 people gathered at the 1,775-foot summit on that rainy day. A century later, the anniversary gathering returned to the cairn at Route 20 and Fred Snow Road, with antique cars representing many decades of the trail’s history. The gathering marked the completion of a mountain road that Lee resident Cortland Bishop and other local Berkshire citizens had campaigned for.
moments.notice: The cairn marks the summit where motorists celebrated the road’s opening.

moments.title: Keystone Arches
moments.text: The Keystone Arches carry the story of mountain travel back to the railroad era. Built around 1840 in Middlefield, Becket and Chester, these stone bridges use neither mortar nor steel reinforcement. A 2.5-mile trail with side spurs brings the bridges into close view. The Western Railroad reached Chester in May 1841. Its arrival transformed Chester Factories into a provisioning stop for trains, and the town’s civic and economic center gradually shifted there. Chester’s Railroad Depot and Museum also houses historic exhibits and restored railroad cars from the 1910s and 1920s.
moments.notice: Look at the stone arches, built without mortar or steel reinforcement.

moments.title: Huntington
moments.text: The West Branch meets the Westfield River at Huntington village, and US 20 follows both waterways through town. The Western Railroad arrived in 1841, attracting settlers and enabling manufacturing near its stop. The railroad stop was then called Chester Village. Streets and even houses straddled town boundaries until neighboring sections of Blandford and Chester were annexed in 1853. Two years later, the town took the name Huntington in honor of Charles P. Huntington. Farther north, the construction of Knightville Dam from 1939 to 1941 removed the villages of Knightville and Indian Hollow.
